builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: τ-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
summary: The benchmark replaces English-only tool-use agent evaluation (tau-bench/tau^3-bench) with natively localized variants spanning German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi across airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains, including culturally appropriate databases and native-expert-refined user simulators. Adoption costs the engineering effort of running the benchmark harness against the production agent and, for languages beyond those released, replicating the native-speaker localization process rather than machine-translating prompts. It can fail by overfitting agent tuning to benchmark-specific phrasings, and its fixed domain set may not cover the reader's actual production tools or languages.
rationale: Teams deploying multilingual tool-using agents should validate with this benchmark before launch, since the paper demonstrates large language-specific regressions that English-only testing cannot detect, though teams operating only in English gain little.
technique: Native multilingual localization of tool-use agent benchmarks

claims.statement: The benchmark replaces English-only tool-use agent evaluation (tau-bench/tau^3-bench) with natively localized variants spanning German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi across airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains, including culturally appropriate databases and native-expert-refined user simulators. Adoption costs the engineering effort of running the benchmark harness against the production agent and, for languages beyond those released, replicating the native-speaker localization process rather than machine-translating prompts. It can fail by overfitting agent tuning to benchmark-specific phrasings, and its fixed domain set may not cover the reader's actual production tools or languages.

Agent pass^4 scores drop by up to 61 points relative to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains across eight evaluated models, revealing performance regressions invisible to English-only evaluation.
